stories.headline: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
stories.title: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
stories.summary: Moscow, Oct 21: US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as US President Donald Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. Witkoff said in televised remarks at the start of the meeting that he hoped to discuss the resumption of the trilateral talks involving the US, Russia and Ukraine that would allow the technical teams to discuss the next steps toward a peace settlement. Putin thanked Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war. The visit came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo. Witkoff's meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to US-led peace efforts, more than 4 ½ years after Russia's army invaded. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion of an imminent breakthrough. Russia and Ukraine are still far apart in their terms for a settlement, as their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes. However, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said late Tuesday that the Oslo meeting, which he attended, “made genuine progress.” Witkoff sees some degree of momentum' in peace efforts Witkoff and Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov also at the table. Witkoff said Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner would join the discussion via a video link. Witkoff said he would inform Putin about Tuesday's talks in Oslo, which he described as “productive,” adding that “there is some degree of momentum.” He thanked Putin for lifting Russia's ban on diesel exports, which angered some US lawmakers, adding that it would help reduce prices for US farmers and truckers. Putin said he was ready to discuss prospects for the restoration of US-Russian economic ties, adding that he is also prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran. Moscow is ready to use its special relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said. Putin was also due to meet Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St Petersburg meeting with other Russian top officials, the Kremlin said. Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a US proposal for UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran. Norway's prime minister sees a possible new phase' in talks Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. “I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning. Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he was visiting the country's Parliament and meeting lawmakers. Witkoff appeared to be making another attempt at overcoming hurdles that have kept a deal out of reach. Zelenskyy said Tuesday that on the agenda were future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction, and the possibility of a ceasefire. Trump said Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks on energy infrastructure but Russia has kept hammering Ukraine's power grid and Kyiv has hit Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Moscow is willing to listen to new US proposals about Ukraine but he doesn't expect any “miracle” from Washington. At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that doesn't happen, “I think it's going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said. Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies. The change happened after Zelenskyy spoke with his American counterparts, including a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Russian attacks kill 5 people and injure 25 others, Ukraine says Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 injured, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city's military administration said. Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said. The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces overnight struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The Russian Defence Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defences overnight intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black Sea. (AP)

stories.headline: Vikramaditya Singh seeks paper ballots, Election Commission reforms
stories.title: Vikramaditya Singh seeks paper ballots, Election Commission reforms
stories.summary: Vikramaditya Singh seeks paper ballots, Election Commission reforms
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Vikramaditya Singh called for paper-ballot elections and reforms within the Election Commission.
The demand intensifies opposition pressure over EVMs, voter-roll revisions and democratic safeguards.

Himachal Pradesh Public Works Department Minister Vikramaditya Singh on Wednesday called for elections to be conducted using paper ballots instead of electronic voting machines and sought reforms within the Election Commission to protect democracy and the Constitution, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Singh also reiterated the opposition's demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the withdrawal of legal immunity granted to Election Commissioners.
Addressing a press conference in Shimla, Singh said the opposition and the public had placed their trust in the Supreme Court.
He stressed that necessary reforms must be introduced to strengthen the democratic system and protect the Constitution.
He was referring to a petition filed in the Supreme Court by members of the INDIA bloc challenging the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and alleged deletion of voters' names.
Singh described the action against opposition leaders and protesters in Delhi as unfortunate, saying the national capital had been turned into “something resembling a military cantonment”.
The Congress MLA expressed concern over the deployment of paramilitary forces and the detention of people.
He alleged that people were being detained at their homes and airports, with some even being held on board aircraft, in an apparent reference to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, PTI reported.
Dipke was detained inside an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on October 10 to prevent him from participating in a CJP protest against Kumar.
Singh said the opposition would continue its struggle to protect democratic rights and the Constitution.

stories.headline: China's tungsten export ban hits defence
stories.title: China's tungsten export ban hits defence
stories.summary: Paris: Prices for tungsten, an ultra-hard metal that is key for the defence industry, have soared to record highs since China restricted exports in mid-2025.The restrictions by the world's top producer of the metal have become a major cause for concern among manufacturers now forced to diversify their supply sources.The Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME Group), one of the world's leading derivatives exchanges, said Monday it will launch a dedicated futures market to meet growing demand for the metal by early next year to increase price transparency.What is tungsten used for? Tungsten has the highest known melting point of any metal at 3,422 Celsius (6,192 Fahrenheit) and is exceptionally hard, almost as hard as diamond, with a density "equivalent to that of gold," according to a CyclOpe report on raw materials.Those properties make it an excellent material for drilling or producing other metals and hard materials, for example in the automotive or aerospace industries, or in mining.It also enables the production of alloys which are highly resistant, notably to corrosion and heat, a boon for sectors such as aerospace as well as defence.China's placeGlobal production of tungsten is estimated 85,000 tonnes in 2025, according to a US government estimate, a fraction of the figure for metals like copper or nickel.CME Group estimates the value of the tungsten market at more than $20 billion dollars as at current market values of around $230 a kilo.As is the case for rare earths, tungsten is another industry critical area where China enjoys a dominant position with some 79 percent of global production.Second place Vietnam at 3.5 percent, according to CyclOpe.A US government estimate says China holds around 53 percent of global reserves.It is also well out in front when it comes to transforming raw tungsten into the industrial metal, accounting for some 86 percent, according to Ofremi, the French observatory of mineral resources for industrial sectors.In April of last year, amid international trade tensions, Beijing tightened export controls on the metal and cut domestic mining quotes.That constricted supplies and sent global prices soaring from less than $500 to more than $3,000 per metric tonne.ConsequencesLast April, Nicolas Dufourcq, CEO of France's public investment bank Bpifrance, warned of possible repercussions for French manufacturers."Tungsten is the key metal used in metal-cutting tools, which must be replaced regularly. Over the past nine months, we have therefore been using our old tools," he addedTo manufacturers wishing to replace these tools, "the Chinese say, 'you're going to buy Chinese cutting tools,'" Dufourcq added.Race on for other sourcesThe rest of the world is straining to find alternative supply sources.Among projects for the extraction, refining, or recycling of strategic minerals supported by the European Union, five involve tungsten, including two mines.They are the El Moto project led by Abenojar Tungsten in Spain, where production is scheduled to begin in early 2029, and the Borralha project led by Mineralia in Portugal.France has long produced tungsten in the southern region of Ariege, at the former Salau mine, which some would like to reopen.In June, France's main employer federation, Medef, said re-opening the facility was a question of national sovereignty.Other projects are being launched or revived around the globe, including the Dolphin Mine on King Island, a small Australian island between Melbourne and Tasmania.Launched in 1917, it ceased operations in 1992 as a result of prices long driven down by Chinese production.Today, "the main challenge is ensuring security of supply outside of China. This makes our project an important part of the equation," said Kevin Pallas, head of Group 6 Metals, which owns the mine.Yet mining production alone will not be sufficient to cut dependence on Chinese refining. 'War' metal?Given its usefulness in military hardware tungsten is sometimes known as a "war metal".Its characteristics make it a useful component for armour-piercing munitions.But it has many other uses.Pallas said that only some 13 percent of annual production is linked to military applications.According to experts behind the CyclOpe report, an annual reference for global raw materials and commodity markets, demand is linked to "global industrial dynamics, particularly in the mining and construction sectors, energy and defence."And those experts see precisely those sectors as enjoying "high growth between now and 2030."

body: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME Group), one of the world's leading derivatives exchanges, said Monday it will launch a dedicated futures market to meet growing demand for the metal by early next year to increase price transparency.
What is tungsten used for?

Tungsten has the highest known melting point of any metal at 3,422 Celsius (6,192 Fahrenheit) and is exceptionally hard, almost as hard as diamond, with a density "equivalent to that of gold," according to a CyclOpe report on raw materials.
Those properties make it an excellent material for drilling or producing other metals and hard materials, for example in the automotive or aerospace industries, or in mining.
It also enables the production of alloys which are highly resistant, notably to corrosion and heat, a boon for sectors such as aerospace as well as defence.
China's placeGlobal production of tungsten is estimated 85,000 tonnes in 2025, according to a US government estimate, a fraction of the figure for metals like copper or nickel.
CME Group estimates the value of the tungsten market at more than $20 billion dollars as at current market values of around $230 a kilo.
As is the case for rare earths, tungsten is another industry critical area where China enjoys a dominant position with some 79 percent of global production.
Second place Vietnam at 3.5 percent, according to CyclOpe.
In April of last year, amid international trade tensions, Beijing tightened export controls on the metal and cut domestic mining quotes.
That constricted supplies and sent global prices soaring from less than $500 to more than $3,000 per metric tonne.

ConsequencesLast April, Nicolas Dufourcq, CEO of France's public investment bank Bpifrance, warned of possible repercussions for French manufacturers." Tungsten is the key metal used in metal-cutting tools, which must be replaced regularly.

Over the past nine months, we have therefore been using our old tools," he addedTo manufacturers wishing to replace these tools, "the Chinese say, 'you're going to buy Chinese cutting tools,'" Dufourcq added.
Race on for other sources.
The rest of the world is straining to find alternative supply sources.
Among projects for the extraction, refining, or recycling of strategic minerals supported by the European Union, five involve tungsten, including two mines.
They are the El Moto project led by Abenojar Tungsten in Spain, where production is scheduled to begin in early 2029, and the Borralha project led by Mineralia in Portugal.
France has long produced tungsten in the southern region of Ariege, at the former Salau mine, which some would like to reopen.
In June, France's main employer federation, Medef, said re-opening the facility was a question of national sovereignty.
Other projects are being launched or revived around the globe, including the Dolphin Mine on King Island, a small Australian island between Melbourne and Tasmania.
Launched in 1917, it ceased operations in 1992 as a result of prices long driven down by Chinese production.
Today, "the main challenge is ensuring security of supply outside of China.
This makes our project an important part of the equation," said Kevin Pallas, head of Group 6 Metals, which owns the mine.
Yet mining production alone will not be sufficient to cut dependence on Chinese refining.
'War' metal?
Given its usefulness in military hardware tungsten is sometimes known as a "war metal".
Its characteristics make it a useful component for armour-piercing munitions.
But it has many other uses.

According to experts behind the CyclOpe report, an annual reference for global raw materials and commodity markets, demand is linked to "global industrial dynamics, particularly in the mining and construction sectors, energy and defence." And those experts see precisely those sectors as enjoying "high growth between now and 2030."

stories.headline: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.title: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.summary: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper. I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger. Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone. Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.This is not principally a banking story. It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.From a Large Economy to a Connected OneIn 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion. By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data. At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance. A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure. By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).The business environment remains a work in progress. Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple. Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceGovernment as a Builder of Digital RailsThe government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service. It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers. Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.The scale is remarkable. As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches. In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore. The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model. Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility. The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome. An account opened is not necessarily an account used. An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions. Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes. It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.That is why grassroots adoption remains central. India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsCovid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations. Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities. It encountered resistance because physical presence was often confused with productivity. The pandemic overturned that assumption. When I moved into enterprise technology in 2020, I watched organisations compress years of digital change into months.At the national level, CoWIN provided scheduling, stock tracking and verifiable certificates for a vaccination programme that had administered more than 220 crore doses by January 2023. India also offered the platform as an open-source digital public good to other countries. It showed that software built for Indian scale could have global relevance.From Indian Innovation to a Global ReferenceIndia’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform. It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure. The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance. Women form the majority in all of Jan Dhan accounts. And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts. Photo by Idrees Mohammed / AFPTurning Access into AgencyThe past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology. I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes. I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive. But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement. The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access. The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity. That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

From Indian Innovation to a Global Reference.

India’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform.
It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure.
The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance.

The past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology.
I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes.
I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.
The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive.
But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.
The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.
India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access.

The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity.
That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The Supreme Court told the Andhra Pradesh poll panel to examine YSRCP complaints.
The directions underscore that secure nomination filing is integral to free and fair elections.
A vacation bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a petition filed by the Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party, or YSRCP.
The party alleged that violence and threats had prevented several of its candidates from filing nomination papers for elections to around 100 urban local bodies.

The bench directed the state election commission to consider complaints submitted by the YSRCP and other candidates, along with supporting material, and decide by Thursday whether to extend the nomination deadline.
It also asked the commission to take all necessary steps to address concerns among the YSRCP and other candidates about free and fair elections in the state.
The court directed the Andhra Pradesh Director General of Police to provide adequate security to candidates and election offices.
It observed that the filing of nomination papers was an essential part of free and fair elections.
The bench clarified that it was not directly intervening in the election process but was allowing the state election commission to consider the party's complaint and take an appropriate decision.
It asked the commission to file a compliance affidavit by October 27, the next date of hearing.
According to PTI, the court said the YS Jagan Mohan Reddy-led party had “made out prima facie case” that several of its candidates had been stopped from filing nomination papers.
The court referred to representations submitted by the party and its candidates, both physically and electronically, as well as video clips and other electronic evidence.

stories.headline: Built for Bharat: How India’s rails changed commerce
stories.title: Built for Bharat: How India’s rails changed commerce
stories.summary: When I think about how India has changed over the past 25 years, I think less about individual policies and more about the foundations that make it possible to build and operate a business at national scale. I spent nearly a decade as CEO of Flipkart, and ecommerce gave me a front-row seat to that change.The past 25 years have covered two important phases in India’s economic journey: Narendra Modi’s tenure as chief minister of Gujarat from 2001 and that as prime minister of India since 2014. What has mattered most to me as a business leader is how much the country’s physical infrastructure, digital systems and ease of doing business have evolved during this period.For example, take a small manufacturer in Surat who wants to sell to a customer in Guwahati. Twenty-five years ago, that could have meant finding a distributor, arranging transportation across multiple state borders, dealing with different tax systems and finding a way to collect payment from a customer she had never met. Today, she can register a business, put her products online, accept digital payment, and reach customers thousands of kilometres away.The difference is not ecommerce alone. It is everything around it. Every order we deliver depends on a road, a payment system, an identity framework, a tax system, a warehouse, and a person who can find the customer’s address. Over the years, each of these pieces has become more connected and, in many cases, more accessible.Also Read: India and the digital quarter-centuryPractical mattersI saw the change particularly clearly after 2014, as investment in physical infrastructure accelerated. India’s national highway network expanded substantially, airport connectivity increased, and infrastructure planning became more integrated. PM Gati Shakti, launched in 2021, brought multiple ministries and infrastructure networks onto a common planning framework.For a business like ours, this matters in practical ways. We can plan fulfilment centres and delivery networks with greater confidence and serve customers well beyond the largest cities.The digital transformation has been even more striking. When we started building Flipkart, cash on delivery was essential because many customers were not comfortable paying online. Today, digital payments are part of everyday commerce. UPI processed more than 24.5 billion transactions in August alone.The number is impressive, but the more important change is what sits behind it. A small merchant can accept a payment without a card machine.A consumer can pay with a phone.A business can build services on an interoperable payment system. India has effectively turned digital payments into everyday economic infrastructure.The same is true of identity and financial inclusion. Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and mobile connectivity have created a different environment for onboarding customers and delivering services. Jan Dhan accounts grew from 147.2 million in 2015 to more than 570 million in 2026, while Aadhaar became a foundational layer for digital identity.Good & Services Tax (GST) was another major change for businesses operating across India. The move to a common indirect tax framework reduced many of the complexities of moving goods across state borders. For ecommerce, where a product can be sold in one state, stored in another, and delivered to a third, that simplification matters enormously. A Flipkart fulfilment centre at Sanpka, Haryana. Photo by Madhu KapparathGrowth enginesWe have seen the impact directly at Flipkart.Today, more than 1.4 million sellers use our platform, many of them outside the major metropolitan centres. Through our Samarth initiative, artisans, weavers and small farmers can find customers in other parts of the country. Our ability to serve customers deep into Tier III and IV India is built not just on our own network, but also on the roads, payments, connectivity and digital systems around us. That is also why I think India’s digital transformation is bigger than simply putting existing services online.GST, UPI, Aadhaar and other digital systems have gradually made economic activity more connected, easier to transact and more visible. India has moved from digitising individual processes towards building shared digital rails on which businesses can innovate.This has also changed the nature of India’s growth opportunity. Domestic consumption has become an increasingly important engine of growth. The Economic Survey estimates that private final consumption accounted for 61.5 percent of GDP in FY26, alongside estimated real GDP growth of 7.4 percent.For businesses, that means the opportunity is not simply to serve India’s largest cities. It is to understand and serve a much broader, more diverse and increasingly aspirational consumer base.No single government or company built this transformation. It is the result of public investment, policy changes, private entrepreneurship, technology, rising consumer aspirations, and millions of Indians adopting new ways of doing things. The government’s role is to build and improve the foundations; business’s role is to build on them.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsProductivity and accessOf course, there is still a lot to do. India needs to create jobs at a much larger scale, particularly in manufacturing and other productive sectors. Logistics costs remain an important competitiveness challenge. We need to invest more deeply in skills as technology changes the nature of work.And AI will add a new dimension to all of this.The next generation of infrastructure will not just be roads and ports.It will include data, compute, connectivity and trusted digital systems. India’s advantage will depend not only on how quickly it adopts AI, but also on how effectively it uses AI to improve productivity, expand opportunity, and help smaller businesses compete.This next phase will be about productivity as much as access. India has spent the last 25 years building many of the rails needed for a modern economy. The opportunity now is to help more people and businesses use those rails to create value.Can a small manufacturer become a national brand? Can an artisan in a remote part of the country find a customer thousands of kilometres away? Can a young entrepreneur build a global technology company from an Indian city outside the traditional centres? Can millions of people use digital infrastructure to participate more fully in the formal economy?We are already seeing examples of each. When Modi first became chief minister of Gujarat in 2001, India was asking whether it could build the foundations needed to support a billion people. Twenty-five years later, the more interesting question is what those billion people will build with them.That, ultimately, is how I see the change. The infrastructure is becoming the foundation. India’s entrepreneurs, workers, consumers, and young people will write the next chapter by building on it.And the manufacturer in Surat? She is already showing us what that future can look like. She is shipping to Guwahati. And there are millions like her.

opening: When I think about how India has changed over the past 25 years, I think less about individual policies and more about the foundations that make it possible to build and operate a business at national scale.
I spent nearly a decade as CEO of Flipkart, and ecommerce gave me a front-row seat to that change.
body: The past 25 years have covered two important phases in India’s economic journey: Narendra Modi’s tenure as chief minister of Gujarat from 2001 and that as prime minister of India since 2014.
What has mattered most to me as a business leader is how much the country’s physical infrastructure, digital systems and ease of doing business have evolved during this period.
For example, take a small manufacturer in Surat who wants to sell to a customer in Guwahati.

Twenty-five years ago, that could have meant finding a distributor, arranging transportation across multiple state borders, dealing with different tax systems and finding a way to collect payment from a customer she had never met.
Today, she can register a business, put her products online, accept digital payment, and reach customers thousands of kilometres away.
The difference is not ecommerce alone.
It is everything around it.
Every order we deliver depends on a road, a payment system, an identity framework, a tax system, a warehouse, and a person who can find the customer’s address.
Over the years, each of these pieces has become more connected and, in many cases, more accessible.
Practical matters.
I saw the change particularly clearly after 2014, as investment in physical infrastructure accelerated.
India’s national highway network expanded substantially, airport connectivity increased, and infrastructure planning became more integrated.
PM Gati Shakti, launched in 2021, brought multiple ministries and infrastructure networks onto a common planning framework.
For a business like ours, this matters in practical ways.
We can plan fulfilment centres and delivery networks with greater confidence and serve customers well beyond the largest cities.
The digital transformation has been even more striking.
When we started building Flipkart, cash on delivery was essential because many customers were not comfortable paying online.
Today, digital payments are part of everyday commerce.
UPI processed more than 24.5 billion transactions in August alone.
The number is impressive, but the more important change is what sits behind it.
A small merchant can accept a payment without a card machine.
A consumer can pay with a phone.
A business can build services on an interoperable payment system.
India has effectively turned digital payments into everyday economic infrastructure.
The same is true of identity and financial inclusion.
Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and mobile connectivity have created a different environment for onboarding customers and delivering services.
Jan Dhan accounts grew from 147.2 million in 2015 to more than 570 million in 2026, while Aadhaar became a foundational layer for digital identity.
Good & Services Tax (GST) was another major change for businesses operating across India.
The move to a common indirect tax framework reduced many of the complexities of moving goods across state borders.
For ecommerce, where a product can be sold in one state, stored in another, and delivered to a third, that simplification matters enormously.
A Flipkart fulfilment centre at Sanpka, Haryana.
Photo by Madhu KapparathGrowth engines.
We have seen the impact directly at Flipkart.
Through our Samarth initiative, artisans, weavers and small farmers can find customers in other parts of the country.
Our ability to serve customers deep into Tier III and IV India is built not just on our own network, but also on the roads, payments, connectivity and digital systems around us.
That is also why I think India’s digital transformation is bigger than simply putting existing services online.
GST, UPI, Aadhaar and other digital systems have gradually made economic activity more connected, easier to transact and more visible.
India has moved from digitising individual processes towards building shared digital rails on which businesses can innovate.
This has also changed the nature of India’s growth opportunity.
Domestic consumption has become an increasingly important engine of growth.
The Economic Survey estimates that private final consumption accounted for 61.5 percent of GDP in FY26, alongside estimated real GDP growth of 7.4 percent.
For businesses, that means the opportunity is not simply to serve India’s largest cities.
It is to understand and serve a much broader, more diverse and increasingly aspirational consumer base.
No single government or company built this transformation.
It is the result of public investment, policy changes, private entrepreneurship, technology, rising consumer aspirations, and millions of Indians adopting new ways of doing things.
The government’s role is to build and improve the foundations; business’s role is to build on them.
Productivity and accessOf course, there is still a lot to do.
India needs to create jobs at a much larger scale, particularly in manufacturing and other productive sectors.
Logistics costs remain an important competitiveness challenge.
We need to invest more deeply in skills as technology changes the nature of work.
And AI will add a new dimension to all of this.
The next generation of infrastructure will not just be roads and ports.
It will include data, compute, connectivity and trusted digital systems.
India’s advantage will depend not only on how quickly it adopts AI, but also on how effectively it uses AI to improve productivity, expand opportunity, and help smaller businesses compete.
This next phase will be about productivity as much as access.
India has spent the last 25 years building many of the rails needed for a modern economy.
The opportunity now is to help more people and businesses use those rails to create value.
Can a small manufacturer become a national brand?
Can an artisan in a remote part of the country find a customer thousands of kilometres away?
Can a young entrepreneur build a global technology company from an Indian city outside the traditional centres?
Can millions of people use digital infrastructure to participate more fully in the formal economy?
We are already seeing examples of each.
When Modi first became chief minister of Gujarat in 2001, India was asking whether it could build the foundations needed to support a billion people.
Twenty-five years later, the more interesting question is what those billion people will build with them.
That, ultimately, is how I see the change.
The infrastructure is becoming the foundation.
India’s entrepreneurs, workers, consumers, and young people will write the next chapter by building on it.
And the manufacturer in Surat?
She is already showing us what that future can look like.
She is shipping to Guwahati.
And there are millions like her.

stories.headline: IMD update: Fresh Bay low-pressure area sets stage for a rain-soaked weekend
stories.title: IMD update: Fresh Bay low-pressure area sets stage for a rain-soaked weekend
stories.summary: India Meteorological Department predicts very heavy showers over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal even as a second ‘low’ could intensify into a major system over the Bay early next week
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A fresh low-pressure area over the south-west Bay of Bengal off the Tamil Nadu coast is likely to set the stage for another spell of intense north-east monsoon rain from the weekend and into early next week.

Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam, Kerala and Mahe, and Lakshadweep are in the firing line as moisture-laden systems threaten to unleash widespread showers, with isolated bouts of very heavy rain.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast isolated very heavy rainfall of 11–20 cm over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal for three days from Thursday.
Kerala and Mahe are in for similar spells on Thursday and again on Saturday and Sunday, while Lakshadweep faces the prospect on Friday and Saturday.
The forecast also flags isolated heavy rainfall of 7–11 cm over South Interior Karnataka for four days from Thursday.
Kerala and Mahe could see heavy spells on Friday and again on Monday and Tuesday; Lakshadweep on Thursday and Sunday; and Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal on Monday.

The impending wet spell follows a punishing 24 hours in which heavy to very heavy rain, exceeding 10 cm in several places, battered parts of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, Rayalaseema, and Kerala and Mahe.
MGR Nagar in Chennai topped the charts with 15 cm, followed by Chennai airport and Alandur with 13 cm each.
The DGP Office in Chennai and Colachel in Kanyakumari district recorded 12 cm apiece, while Chennai city, Kollam in Kerala and Tada in Tirupati district received 11 cm each.
Aliyar in Coimbatore rounded off the list with 10 cm.
The larger atmospheric setting is also falling into place for a vigorous rain spell.

A favourable pulse of the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) appears to be working in tandem with the positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), helping propel circulations into the South Peninsula towards a weekend crescendo.
